title: A Lament for the Princes of Israel
summary: Ezekiel is told to sing a funeral song for Judah's royal house. In the first picture a lioness raises two cubs who become man-eating lions, and both are trapped and dragged away, one to Egypt and one to Babylon. In the second, the mother is a fruitful vine with branches fit for a king's scepter, uprooted, burned, and replanted in the desert until no ruler's branch remains.
story: Chapter 18 insisted that each generation answers for itself. Chapter 19 turns to the kings, the men who were supposed to shepherd Judah and who instead led it toward ruin. The exiles still hoped that the house of David would recover, that a king would rise and the story would bend back toward glory. Ezekiel answers that hope with a funeral song sung before the funeral. The royal line God promised to David in 2 Samuel 7 is about to be cut down, and the chapter mourns it in advance. The book will not leave the question there: in chapters 34 and 37 God promises a shepherd from David's line who will rule rightly. But first the old monarchy must be buried.
historical:
The chapter looks back over the last kings of Judah. After good King Josiah was killed at Megiddo in 609 BC, his son Jehoahaz reigned only three months before Pharaoh Necho of Egypt deposed him and carried him off to Egypt, where he died (2 Kings 23:31-34). He is almost certainly the first cub, led away with hooks to Egypt (verse 4). The identity of the second cub, brought to the king of Babylon (verse 9), is debated. Many interpreters think of Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC after a three-month reign (2 Kings 24:8-15), who was Ezekiel's fellow exile. Others think of Zedekiah, the last king, captured in 586 BC, blinded, and taken to Babylon (2 Kings 25:4-7), which would make the chapter partly a prophecy of what was still to come. A few suggest Jehoiakim.

The mother lioness may be the nation of Judah or the royal house as a whole. Some readers see a particular queen mother, Hamutal, who bore both Jehoahaz and Zedekiah (2 Kings 23:31; 24:18). In the vine section, the main branch from which fire goes out (verse 14) is usually taken to be Zedekiah, whose rebellion against Babylon brought the final catastrophe on the city.
cultural:
A lament, qinah in Hebrew, was a funeral song, often sung by professional mourning women and by relatives at a burial. It had a recognizable sound: a limping rhythm in which a longer line is followed by a shorter one, as if the voice breaks. Ezekiel's hearers would have known from the first line that someone was being mourned. To sing a dirge over a royal house that was still standing was a shocking act, the equivalent of reading the obituary of a living man in his presence.

Both images come from Israel's own traditions about its kings. The lion was the emblem of the tribe of Judah from Jacob's blessing onward (Genesis 49:9), and ancient Near Eastern kings liked to picture themselves as lions. The detail of captives led with hooks reflects real practice: Assyrian reliefs show prisoners led by ropes attached to rings in their lips or noses, and wild animals caught in pits and nets were paraded before kings. The vine was Israel's standard picture of itself as God's planting (Psalm 80:8-16; Isaiah 5:1-7), and the east wind was the scorching desert wind that could wither a harvest in a day.
literary: The chapter is a poem in two panels, framed at the start by the command to take up a lament and at the end by the note that this is a lament and will be used as one. The lion panel (verses 2 to 9) follows a pattern repeated twice: the mother raises a cub, he learns to tear prey and devours men, the nations hear, he is trapped and led away. The repetition makes the fall of the second cub feel inevitable. The vine panel (verses 10 to 14) moves from abundance to ruin in a few lines: planted by water, towering and fruitful, then uprooted, dried, burned, and replanted in a dry and thirsty land, which is exile. Verse 7 has a difficult Hebrew text; read literally it speaks of the lion knowing widows, and many translations, including the BSB, follow a slight emendation that yields broke down their strongholds.

outline.t: A lament for the princes: the mother lioness
The first cub, trapped and led to Egypt
The second cub, caged and brought to Babylon
The mother as a fruitful vine with royal branches
The vine uprooted, burned, and planted in the wilderness

doctrines.note: Kings who were meant to protect their people instead devoured them, and their power could not save them from judgment. The chapter shows God's verdict falling on the most privileged office in Israel.
By mourning the end of every ruler's scepter (verse 14), the chapter creates the vacuum that the promise of a true Davidic shepherd will later fill (Ezekiel 34:23-24; 37:24-25).
Scripture gives grief its own form. The lament lets Israel mourn honestly what it has lost, even when the loss is deserved, rather than skipping straight to explanation.

words.note: Qinah, a dirge or funeral lament. The word frames the chapter (verses 1 and 14). It is the same kind of song David sang over Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:17), and it gives the book of Lamentations its character. Ezekiel uses the form again for Tyre and Egypt in later chapters.
Kephir, a young lion in its prime, strong enough to hunt on its own. The word pictures the princes at the height of their power, which makes their capture more striking.

Shevet, a rod or staff, and so a ruler's scepter (verses 11 and 14). The same word can mean tribe. The chapter's final grief is that no branch remains fit to be a scepter. Readers have often heard an echo of Genesis 49:10, where the scepter is promised not to depart from Judah.

christ: The chapter ends with no scepter left. That is the low point from which the promise of a new David rises. Ezekiel himself will speak of a tender sprig planted on a high mountain (17:22-24) and of one shepherd, God's servant David, over a restored people (34:23-24). The New Testament presents Jesus as that son of David and calls him the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5), but a lion of a different kind: in the same vision he appears as a Lamb that was slain. Where Judah's last kings learned to tear prey and devour men, the promised king gives his own life for his people. The link between this lament and Christ is not a prediction in the poem itself; it is the shape of the larger story, in which the collapse of the old royal line makes room for the king God himself provides.
questions: Why might God tell a prophet to sing a funeral song for something that has not yet fully died? What does grief do that explanation cannot?
The young lions learned to tear prey and devour men. How does power change the people who hold it, and where have you seen it happen?
The vine is replanted in a dry and thirsty land. What does it look like to live faithfully in a season when what you hoped for has been uprooted?
